title: An online shop for a ceramics studio
metaTitle: A ceramics shop built around the object
excerpt: Show the ceramic at the scale of a hand, with glaze, size, and lead time, then use a short checkout. Skip the marketplace grid.
alt: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper. A ceramics shop has to be this specific about glaze and scale before anyone pays.
caption: A line written with care. The cup page needs the same care. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first screen of a ceramics product page show?
faqs.answer: The piece, large enough that the glaze reads, plus the price and whether it is in the studio or made when ordered. A second image should answer scale, with dimensions in text nearby. Care, such as food safety and the dishwasher, belongs on the page rather than in a footer policy.

faqs.question: How long should checkout be for a small ceramics shop?
faqs.answer: Short. Ask for email, shipping address, a shipping method with a price, and payment. Baymard's benchmark describes an ideal flow around 12 to 14 form elements, against a much longer US average. Show fragile-shipping cost before the card, and let a one-time buyer check out as a guest.

faqs.question: Should one-of-one pieces stay in the grid after they sell?
faqs.answer: Mark them sold and then remove them from the category. A dead button left in the grid looks like a stock error. Do not treat a singular piece as a variant of a production cup.

markdown:
A ceramics studio ecommerce website has one job before the cart: show the object at the scale of a hand, with the glaze, the lip, and the weight made legible. Checkout comes after that, and it should be short. A grid that looks like a marketplace will shrink the work into a tile and teach people to compare you on price alone.

Build the product page around what a person needs to see and hold, then give them a direct way to pay. Keep the shop specific to this studio. Do not borrow the filters, the badges, or the endless related-product rail from a site that sells everything.

## The page starts with the object in the hand

The first screen is the piece, large enough that the glaze reads, with one fact beside it: the name, the price, and whether it is in the studio now or made when ordered. A cup and a lamp do not share a layout that hides those facts under a promotional banner. The object is the banner.

Show scale on purpose. A second image puts the piece next to a hand, a table setting, or another object whose size people know. Dimensions in centimeters or inches sit in text near that image, not in a tab nobody opens. Weight belongs there too when the piece is meant to be used, because a bowl that looks delicate and arrives heavy is a surprise you can prevent. If you ship a set, say how many pieces and whether the photograph is one or the set.

Glaze is the product. Name it in words, and show it in more than one light if the color shifts. A single white-background crop that kills the variation is a different object from the one in the studio. The photography piece that follows this one is about keeping that crop consistent. The page's job is to give the photograph enough room, and then get out of the way with the facts.

Care is a short list: dishwasher or not, food safe or not, what to avoid. Those lines prevent returns and they prevent disappointment. They are part of the product, not a footer policy.

## A shop, not a marketplace grid

The collection page can show several pieces. It should still look like one studio. That means one crop logic, one background family, and type that matches the work. A masonry grid of mixed orientations, sale badges, and "customers also bought" from unrelated makers makes the shop look unfinished even when the pots are excellent.

Do not add a filter for every adjective you can think of. If you have eight bowls, a filter is a puzzle. If you have a hundred pieces across cups, plates, and lamps, then offer the categories a buyer actually uses: form, and maybe glaze family. Leave "mood" and "aesthetic" out. They do not help someone find a cup that fits their hand.

Related pieces, if you show them, are other works from this studio that a buyer of this bowl might want, chosen by you, not by a similarity score on price. Three is enough. A rail of twenty is a marketplace habit, and it pulls attention off the decision they were about to make.

Hanabi's public project Down the Cove was an ecommerce migration and redesign: the shop had to keep selling while the pages became specific to the brand. The same discipline applies here. Move the catalog without turning it into a generic storefront. The pieces are the brand.

Search on a small catalog can be a simple field, or it can wait. A studio with forty SKUs needs clear categories more than it needs a search engine. Build search when you can no longer point a new colleague at the right page in one sentence.

## Variants without a messy page

Glaze, size, and the occasional one-of-one piece are the variants that matter. Show glaze as a named choice with a swatch that matches the photograph, and change the hero image when the glaze changes. A buyer who selects "ash" and still sees the "iron" photograph will not trust the checkout.

One-of-one work should not pretend to be a variant of a production cup. Give it a page that says it is singular, and remove it cleanly when it sells. A sold piece left in the grid with a dead button looks like a stock error. A short "sold" state, then an exit from the category, is enough.

Made-to-order is a variant of time, not of color. State the lead time in the first screen, in words: "made for you, ships in four to six weeks" if that is true. Do not hide it until after payment. If the lead time changes with the season, a person updates the sentence. A countdown you do not mean is worse than a plain range.

Sets and singles need a clear price for each. If the pair is the offer, do not make them add two singles and wonder why the glaze does not match. Say whether a pair is matched. Ceramics buyers care about that, and they cannot tell from a thumbnail.

## A short checkout after a clear page

The product page did the persuading. Checkout collects what you need to pack a fragile object and nothing else. Baymard Institute's [cart abandonment research](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) puts the average documented abandonment rate at 70.22 percent across 50 studies, updated in 2025. A large share of that is browsing: in Baymard's study, 42 percent of US online shoppers had abandoned because they were just looking or not ready. The losses you can affect sit in the rest of the list. Extra costs such as shipping, tax, and fees are cited by 40 percent. Being told to create an account is 18 percent. A checkout that felt too long or complicated is 17 percent. Not being able to see the total up front is 12 percent.

Baymard also describes an ideal checkout as about 12 to 14 form elements, or 7 to 8 if you count only fields, against an average US checkout of 23.48 elements and 14.88 fields. A ceramics studio does not need the average. Ask for email, shipping name and address, a shipping method with a price, and payment. Ask for a phone number only if the carrier or you will actually use it for delivery day. Leave "how did you hear about us" off the path.

Show the shipping cost before the card. Fragile packing and rural delivery are real costs, and they should appear as soon as the address is known, not as a surprise on the last step. If you cannot ship a platter to a region, say so on the product page, not after they have typed a card number.

Guest checkout is the default for a one-time piece. Offer an account after payment if they want to hear about the next firing. Do not require a password in order to buy a cup.

## Trust, packing, and the note after payment

People are handing you money for an object they have not held. The page earns that with the photographs, the dimensions, and a plain returns line. Baymard lists an unsatisfactory returns policy at 13 percent of US shoppers in that abandonment study, and distrust about the card at 19 percent. Use a payment provider they can recognize, and say who processes the card. Put the returns line where the total is: how many days, who pays return shipping, and what "damage in transit" means. A ceramic that arrives in pieces is not a normal apparel return. Say what you will do.

The confirmation page and the email repeat the lead time, the shipping window, and how to reach a person. They do not upsell a random second object in the moment they are wondering whether the first will arrive whole. If you pack a note in the box, that note is a person's words. Do not generate a different personality for the insert than the one on the site.

For a studio that also sells in person, the site should not undercut the gallery by accident with a different price. One price, stated. If wholesale is different, it lives behind a conversation, not a public discount code on the cup page.

If you want to see how a shop can stay specific to the maker, look at Hanabi's [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful pattern is a product page that respects the object and a checkout that respects the buyer's time.

## What to leave off

Leave off urgency banners that are not true. "Only one left" is acceptable when the piece is one-of-one and the count is real. It is not a style choice for a cup you can make again next month. Leave off reviews that are about a different glaze, lumped under the product as if they were this one. Leave off a blog post in the middle of the buy box.

Leave the marketplace chrome: star histograms as the main event, sponsored rows, and a chat widget that opens before the glaze has loaded. If you want a question channel, a link to write a person is enough at this size. A bot that answers "is it food safe?" from a guess is a liability. Put food-safe in the facts so the bot is unnecessary.

Keep the catalog editable by the studio. A page builder piled under the product will make the next firing's update a project. A small set of fields, name, price, glaze, lead time, dimensions, and images, is the system they will use. Hanabi builds this kind of shop in Next.js, React, and TypeScript, with the content in a place the studio can update without a redeploy for every sentence, and the pages still able to stay fast.

## Mobile, and the photograph's job

Most of these buyers will arrive on a phone. The first screen still has to be the object, not a menu and a cookie wall. The price and the made-to-order line stay visible when they scroll to the details. Tap targets for glaze choices need to be large enough that a wrong glaze is not the default outcome.

The next decision is how those photographs are made so the grid feels like one bench. [Product photography for a ceramics studio](/blog/product-photography-for-a-ceramics-studio) is the piece to read next. Crop, background, and the in-hand frame are what keep this shop from looking like a folder of unrelated pictures.
